lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Composition of the Solar System and the Outer Planets

pages.body:
In Basic 7 you studied the four rocky planets closest to the Sun. Beyond Mars lie four planets so large that the Earth looks like a small bead beside them.

- What do you already know about the planets beyond Mars?
- Why do you think those planets are much colder than the Earth?

The solar system is the Sun together with everything that moves around it. In this lesson we describe what the solar system is made of, identify the four outer planets and study the properties that make each one special.

We begin with the members of the solar system.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What the solar system is made of

pages.title: What the solar system is made of
pages.body:
| **Member** | **Description** |
|---|---|
| The Sun | A star at the centre of the solar system. It holds almost all the mass of the system and its gravity keeps every other member in orbit |
| Planets | Eight large bodies that orbit the Sun. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the inner planets. Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are the outer planets |
| Moons | Natural satellites that orbit planets. The Earth has one moon and the outer planets have many |
| Dwarf planets | Small round bodies that orbit the Sun but have not cleared their paths of other objects. Pluto and Ceres are examples |
| Asteroids | Rocky objects, most of which orbit the Sun in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter |
| Comets | Bodies of ice and dust that grow a bright tail when they come close to the Sun |
| Meteoroids | Small pieces of rock or metal in space. One that burns in the air of the Earth is seen as a meteor, or shooting star |

The asteroid belt separates the inner planets from the outer planets. The inner planets are small and rocky. The outer planets are very large, have no solid surface that a spacecraft could land on, have many moons and all have rings.

Next we meet the four outer planets in order from the Sun.

pages.title: The outer planets
pages.body: Jupiter and Saturn are called gas giants because they are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune are called ice giants because, beneath their hydrogen and helium, they contain large amounts of water, ammonia and methane in a thick, cold, slushy form.

| **Property** | **Jupiter** | **Saturn** | **Uranus** | **Neptune** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Position from the Sun | Fifth | Sixth | Seventh | Eighth |
| Distance from the Sun | About 778 million km | About 1 430 million km | About 2 870 million km | About 4 500 million km |
| Diameter | About 143 000 km | About 120 000 km | About 51 000 km | About 49 500 km |
| Time for one orbit | About 12 Earth years | About 29 Earth years | About 84 Earth years | About 165 Earth years |
| Time for one rotation | About 10 hours | About 11 hours | About 17 hours | About 16 hours |
| Type | Gas giant | Gas giant | Ice giant | Ice giant |
| Colour | Orange and white bands | Pale yellow | Pale blue green | Deep blue |
Now we look at what makes each planet different from the others.

questions.q: Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of
questions.e: Jupiter and Saturn are called gas giants because they are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Properties peculiar to each outer planet

pages.title: Properties peculiar to each outer planet
pages.body:
- Jupiter is the largest planet. About eleven Earths would fit across its width. It spins faster than any other planet, so it has the shortest day. Its Great Red Spot is a giant storm that has been seen for hundreds of years. It has more than 90 known moons, including Ganymede, the largest moon in the solar system.
- Saturn is the second largest planet and is famous for its bright, wide rings made of pieces of ice and rock. It is the least dense planet, less dense than water. It has more known moons than any other planet. Its largest moon, Titan, has a thick atmosphere.
- Uranus spins on its side, so it seems to roll around the Sun like a ball. Methane gas in its atmosphere gives it a pale blue green colour. It has the coldest atmosphere of all the planets, about 224 degrees below zero Celsius, and faint dark rings.
- Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun and takes about 165 Earth years to make one orbit. It has the fastest winds in the solar system, up to about 2 000 km per hour. Its deep blue colour comes from methane. Its largest moon, Triton, orbits in the opposite direction to the spin of the planet.

[[pic: Scale drawing of Jupiter, Saturn with its rings, Uranus tilted on its side and Neptune, shown in order from the Sun with the Earth drawn beside them for comparison of size.]]

The farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its path, the slower it moves and the longer its year. This is why a year on Neptune is far longer than a year on Jupiter.

> **Did you know?** The number of known moons of the outer planets keeps rising as telescopes improve, so the figures in different books may not agree.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Why There Is No Life on the Outer Planets and How to Model Them

pages.body:
The Earth has liquid water, air with oxygen, a solid surface and a gentle temperature. Imagine a planet with no ground to stand on, winds faster than any storm on the Earth and a temperature colder than any freezer.

- Could a plant, a fish or a human live on such a planet?
- What would be the first problem a living thing would face there?

Life as we know it needs liquid water, a suitable temperature, a source of energy and a safe surface or ocean to live in. In this lesson we explain why the outer planets do not meet these needs, and we plan a model of the outer solar system.

We begin with the conditions that make the outer planets hostile to life.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Why there is no life on the outer planets

pages.title: Why there is no life on the outer planets
pages.body:
| **Condition** | **Why it prevents life** |
|---|---|
| No solid surface | The outer planets are balls of gas and slushy liquid. There is no ground for plants to root in or for animals to live on |
| Extreme cold | They are very far from the Sun, so their cloud tops are far below the freezing point of water. Water cannot stay liquid there |
| Very little sunlight | Sunlight is too weak for plants to make food by photosynthesis |
| Poisonous atmosphere | The atmosphere is mostly hydrogen and helium with methane and ammonia. There is no oxygen for breathing |
| Crushing pressure | Deep inside the planets the pressure of the gas above is great enough to crush any living thing |
| Violent weather | Storms larger than the Earth and winds of hundreds or thousands of kilometres per hour blow all the time |

For these reasons scientists do not expect life on Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus or Neptune. Some of their moons, however, are of great interest. Europa, a moon of Jupiter, and Enceladus, a moon of Saturn, appear to have oceans of liquid water beneath their icy crusts, and spacecraft are being sent to study them.

Next we see how scientists collected this information.

questions.q: Which of the following is a reason why there is no life on the outer planets?
o: They are too close to the Sun
questions.e: The outer planets are very large, have no solid surface that a spacecraft could land on, have many moons and all have rings.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How we know about the outer planets

pages.title: How we know about the outer planets
pages.body:
The outer planets are too far away to visit in person. Scientists study them with telescopes and with spacecraft that carry cameras and instruments. The two Voyager spacecraft flew past the outer planets, and Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft that has visited Uranus and Neptune. The Juno spacecraft has been orbiting Jupiter since 2016, and the Cassini spacecraft orbited Saturn for thirteen years.

Finally we plan a model that shows the order and the relative sizes of the outer planets.

pages.title: Constructing a model of the outer solar system
pages.body:
1. Collect materials such as old newspapers, balloons, clay, calabashes, oranges, paint, string and cardboard.
2. Choose a scale for size. If Jupiter is a ball 14 cm wide, make Saturn 12 cm wide, Uranus 5 cm wide and Neptune 5 cm wide.
3. Shape each planet and paint it. Give Jupiter orange and white bands with a red spot, Saturn a pale yellow colour, Uranus a pale blue green colour and Neptune a deep blue colour.
4. Cut a flat ring from cardboard and fix it around Saturn. Fix Uranus so that it is tilted on its side.
5. Hang or place the planets in the correct order from a large yellow circle that stands for the Sun.
6. Label each planet and write two of its properties on a card beside it.
7. Explain to the class what your model shows well and what it cannot show, such as the true distances between the planets.
> **Did you know?** If the Sun were a football in the centre of a school field, Neptune would be a small bead about 700 metres away.

pages.body:
- The solar system is made up of the Sun, eight planets, moons, dwarf planets, asteroids, comets and meteoroids.
- The outer planets in order from the Sun are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. They lie beyond the asteroid belt.
- Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
- Jupiter is the largest planet and has the Great Red Spot. Saturn has bright rings and is the least dense planet. Uranus spins on its side. Neptune is the farthest planet and has the fastest winds.
- The outer planets all have rings and many moons, and they take from about 12 to about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
- There is no life on the outer planets because they have no solid surface, are extremely cold, receive little sunlight, have poisonous atmospheres without oxygen, and have crushing pressure and violent storms.
- A model of the outer solar system shows the order, colours and relative sizes of the planets but not their true distances.
